Prediction-powered inference for a mean

Source: R/core-stats-estimate.R
hr_ppi.Rd

Estimates the mean of an outcome from many units that have only a model's prediction and a few that also have the true value, without inheriting the model's bias. Use it to report a judge-scored accuracy, or any rate where a model labelled everything and people labelled a sample.

Usage

hr_ppi(
  yhat_unlabelled,
  yhat_labelled,
  y_labelled,
  pi = NULL,
  conf = 0.95,
  tune = TRUE
)

Arguments

yhat_unlabelled

Predictions on the units without a true value.

yhat_labelled

Predictions on the labelled units.

y_labelled

True values on the labelled units (numeric or logical).

pi

Optional probability with which each labelled unit was chosen for labelling, in (0, 1].

conf

Confidence level.

tune

Whether to tune lambda (PPI++). FALSE fixes it at 1.

Value

A one-row data frame: estimate, se, lower, upper, n (labelled), N (unlabelled), lambda and method ("ppi", "ppi++", "dsl" or "dsl tuned").

Details

With tune = FALSE this is the estimator of Angelopoulos et al. (2023):

estimate = mean(yhat_U) + mean(y_L - yhat_L)
variance = var(yhat_U) / N + var(y_L - yhat_L) / n

where U are the N unlabelled units and L the n labelled ones. The second term (the rectifier) removes the predictions' bias.

With tune = TRUE (PPI++, Angelopoulos, Duchi and Zrnic 2023) the predictions are scaled by lambda:

estimate = mean(y_L) + lambda * (mean(yhat_U) - mean(yhat_L))
lambda   = cov(y_L, yhat_L) / ((1 + n / N) * var(yhat_L))

clipped to [0, 1]. lambda = 0 is the mean of the labelled units alone and lambda = 1 the untuned estimator, so tuning never does worse than either in large samples: poor predictions get little weight.

When pi is given and varies, the labelled units were drawn with unequal probabilities from the whole set (U and L together, N + n units), and the rectifier is inverse-probability weighted as in design-based supervised learning (Egami et al. 2023). Each unit gets the pseudo-outcome

ytilde_i = lambda * yhat_i + R_i * (y_i - lambda * yhat_i) / pi_i

with R_i = 1 for labelled units, and the estimate is the mean of ytilde over all N + n units with variance var(ytilde) / (N + n). Tuning chooses the lambda in [0, 1] that minimises that variance. Equal pi gives the unweighted form above.

The interval is normal: estimate +/- z * se.

References

Angelopoulos, A. N., Bates, S., Fannjiang, C., Jordan, M. I. and Zrnic, T. (2023). Prediction-powered inference. Science 382(6671), 669-674.

Angelopoulos, A. N., Duchi, J. C. and Zrnic, T. (2023). PPI++: Efficient prediction-powered inference. arXiv:2311.01453.

Egami, N., Hinck, M., Stewart, B. M. and Wei, H. (2023). Using imperfect surrogates for downstream inference: design-based supervised learning for social science applications of large language models. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36.

See also

Other statistics: hr_agreement(), hr_alt_test(), hr_ht_estimate(), hr_prop_ci()

Examples

set.seed(2)
truth <- rbinom(2100, 1, 0.3)
# A judge that is right 85% of the time.
judged <- ifelse(runif(2100) < 0.85, truth, 1 - truth)
lab <- 1:100
hr_ppi(judged[-lab], judged[lab], truth[lab])
#>   estimate         se     lower     upper   n    N  lambda method
#> 1 0.318293 0.03625286 0.2472387 0.3893473 100 2000 0.59236  ppi++
hr_ppi(judged[-lab], judged[lab], truth[lab], tune = FALSE)
#>   estimate         se     lower     upper   n    N lambda method
#> 1    0.324 0.04142234 0.2428137 0.4051863 100 2000      1    ppi
